standard.title: Generate, test, iterate and communicate design ideas
standard.description: apply innovation and enterprise skills to generate, test, iterate and communicate design ideas, processes and solutions, including using digital tools
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can generate, test, iterate and communicate design ideas, processes and solutions (AC9TDE8P02). They have experience with ideation techniques, modelling and design documentation. They have not yet applied innovation and enterprise skills, reimagined designs to feature emerging technologies, or used the full range of technical drawing and 3D modelling/prototyping tools at this level.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students apply innovation and enterprise skills to generate, test, iterate and communicate design ideas and solutions — using analysis of benefits and constraints, a range of modelling and prototyping techniques, and appropriate technical documentation for an intended audience.

nodes.label: Generating ideas with innovation and enterprise thinking
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use innovation and enterprise thinking to generate design concepts, including reimagining existing designs and incorporating emerging technologies.
nodes.minimum_width: Generate at least two distinct design concepts using at least one innovation or enterprise technique; concepts should be different approaches, not variants of the same solution.
nodes.typical_width: Apply innovation and enterprise skills — brainstorming novel ideas inspired by nature, transforming a solution for a target market, reimagining designs with emerging technologies — to generate a range of design concepts; consider competing variables (weight, strength, price, sustainability, user needs, community consultation) that may shape or constrain the concepts.
wider: Use nature-inspired design (biomimicry) as an ideation framework — generate concepts that translate a natural mechanism or structure into a designed solution
Generate concepts that respond to an identified enterprise opportunity — explain what market gap or user need each concept addresses and how it would be communicated to a target market
Design wearable technology concepts that incorporate emerging technologies (e.g. biometric sensing) to provide independence for elderly or health-focused users
success_criteria: At least two distinct design concepts are generated — not variations of the same approach
At least one concept reflects innovation or enterprise thinking beyond conventional solutions

nodes.label: Functional, structural and aesthetic analysis
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can undertake functional, structural and aesthetic analysis of design ideas, identifying benefits and constraints for different communities and environments.
nodes.minimum_width: Analyse one design idea against at least two of the three dimensions (functional, structural, aesthetic); identify one benefit and one constraint.
nodes.typical_width: Undertake functional, structural and aesthetic analysis of multiple design ideas; identify benefits and constraints for different communities and environments; consider how the same design might need to be adapted for a different context (e.g. for use in a different region or for accessibility requirements).
wider: Analyse a design for suitability in a challenging environment — for example, how skyscraper design adapts structurally and functionally for earthquake zones such as Japan

Analyse a design for accessibility across different user populations — identify what functional or structural changes would be required for the design to serve users with different physical requirements
Compare the same design brief resolved for two different cultural or geographic contexts — analyse how different constraints produce different design solutions

response_modes.reason: Three-dimension analysis (functional, structural, aesthetic) requires a systematic framework — students who analyse without structure tend to describe the design rather than evaluate it against these specific lenses. A scaffold (what does it do? → how does it hold up? → how does it look and feel to use?) produces genuine analysis.

success_criteria: Analysis addresses at least two of the three dimensions explicitly
Identifies a genuine benefit and a genuine constraint — not just positive descriptions
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who analyse design ideas on only one dimension produce prototypes at N3 that test one factor and ignore the others — the prototype does not represent the full design intent and N4 communication cannot justify multi-factor decisions that were never made.

nodes.label: Producing drawings, models and prototypes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can produce drawings, models and prototypes using appropriate techniques and digital tools to explore and develop design ideas.
nodes.minimum_width: Produce at least one visual or physical representation of a design idea using a drawing technique or modelling tool; explain what aspect of the design the representation communicates.
nodes.typical_width: Produce multiple representations of design ideas using a range of techniques — technical drawings (perspective, orthogonal), digital imaging, 3D modelling or 3D printing, or AR modelling; use prototypes to explore aesthetic considerations and test functional ideas; explain what each representation communicates that the others don't.
wider: Produce multiple prototypes that show an understanding of competing aesthetic considerations — explain how each prototype prioritises different aesthetic factors and what user feedback would help choose between them
Use 3D printing or AR modelling software to prototype a design — explain what this representation reveals that 2D drawing cannot
Produce a technical drawing (orthogonal and perspective) of the same design and explain how each representation serves a different stage or audience in the design process

response_modes.reason: Prototype fidelity develops through accumulation — students who have only produced sketches cannot judge what a physical prototype tests that a sketch doesn't. Multiple representation types build the ability to match representation type to design purpose.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Multiple representation types — technical drawing, 3D modelling, physical prototype — each reveal different aspects of a design. Students who can articulate what each representation communicates have rich design communication fluency.
success_criteria: Produces at least one representation with sufficient detail that another person could understand the design
Can explain what aspect of the design the representation communicates

nodes.label: Communicating design ideas and processes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can communicate design ideas, processes and solutions using appropriate technical language and documentation for an intended audience.
nodes.minimum_width: Document at least one stage of a design process with sufficient detail and appropriate technical language for the intended audience to follow.
nodes.typical_width: Develop documentation (e.g. a digital portfolio) that communicates each step of the design process using appropriate technical terms, images and text; justify design decisions made at key stages; ensure communication is tailored to the intended audience.
wider: Produce a digital portfolio with images and text that clearly communicates each step of a design process — explain how the documentation decisions were made for the intended audience
Justify design decisions in the documentation including trade-offs made, alternatives considered, and sustainability rationale
Develop a design communication package for an enterprise context — pitching the design concept to a target market audience rather than a technical audience
success_criteria: At least one design decision is justified — not just described
